To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

MUC1 is an oncogenic molecule that promotes lung carcinogenesis by inhibiting epiregulin production in fibroblastic cells and that MUC1 deficiency enhances epiregulin expression and EGFR signaling in lung cancer cells to promote carcinogenesis.
MUC1 deficiency promotes lung carcinogenesis in mice by potentiating EREG-induced EGFR activation.

Muc1 knockout mice are more susceptible to carcinogen-induced lung tumor development and that this susceptibility involves a feedback loop between MUC1 expression in fibroblast cells and epiregulin expression in malignant cells that activates EGFR.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Muc1 KO mice are more sensitive to NNK-induced lung carcinogenesis, and Muc1 KO lung tumor tissues show enhanced EGFR signaling and increased EREG expression.

MUC1 is a promiscuous protein with both tumor suppressive and tumor promoting functions, and that the net effect of MUC1 on carcinogenesis depends on the specific cell type and the tumor microenvironment.
MUC1 deficiency promotes lung carcinogenesis by increasing EREG expression, which in turn activates the EGFR signaling pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Muc1 deficiency in lung cancer may be detrimental, and that Muc1 is a potential biomarker for lung carcinogenesis and prognosis.
MUC1 may be an oncogenic factor in lung carcinogenesis.
MUC1 may have a dual role in cancer development and that MUC1 deficiency may have different outcomes depending on the cell type.
